utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecution versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Matthias Neuner and Daryl Mundis, assisted today by Andres Vatter, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President, good day, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, and Muriel Cauvin, legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we have the appearances for the other Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: For Mr. Kubura this morning, Mr. Rodney Dixon and Mr. Nermin Mulalic. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present. This is our 172nd day. I'd like to greet the members of the Prosecution, Defence counsel, some of whom are missing, the accused, and everyone else in and around the courtroom. We will be continuing with the cross-examination of a witness today. He must be waiting, and I will now ask the usher to bring him into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Neuner.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning everybody in and around the courtroom. I just want to make a short announcement while the witness is coming to the courtroom. The Prosecution intends to use two new documents this morning. My colleague Mr. Mundis has announced yesterday that this might occur. I have exchanged yesterday also mobile telephone numbers with the Defence counsel and I have made two calls in order to do everything possible to give advance notice that documents are coming, and this morning my understanding is they have been delivered as late as when we assembled here in the courtroom. I just want to give notice about this fact. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If I can confirm that we have this morning received two new documents. I know my learned friends were under some time pressure, but the first time I did manage to get these documents was this morning, and I've been able to look at them now for the first time, and on first glance we will wish to address Your Honours on whether these documents can be shown to the witness or not at the appropriate time. So we would ask at that stage if the witness could be asked to leave the courtroom so that we can submit to Your Honours what our position is on those documents. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Good day, sir. I'd like to ask you to leave the courtroom for a few minutes because there is a procedural issue that we have to deal with first. The usher will escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to Mr. Dixon, the Prosecution has told us that yesterday during the hearing the Prosecution said that they would be presenting new documents. The Prosecution has said that yesterday evening, they tried to contact the Defence by phoning their mobile number. Apparently they weren't able to reach you, and you only received the documents in question this morning. So that's the situation. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can advise that we did receive mobile messages very late last night but those messages didn't refer to which documents would be regarded as the new ones. In fact, Mr. Neuner said at that stage he did not know which were the documents he was going to use today. So the first time we found out about these documents was this morning. That's when he knew exactly which documents would be used. And I've only been able to briefly look through them now. My proposal would be that Mr. Neuner should, when the appropriate time comes in his cross-examination, if he does wish to still use the documents, to submit to Your Honours at that point what the reason is for wanting to show the document. If it's credibility, on what basis he wishes to challenge the credibility of the witness and/or if it is memory refreshing. Perhaps it's premature to consider the question now. I have some questions to ask the witness on behalf of Mr. Kubura, and then Mr. Neuner will proceed, and based on the answers the witness gives, perhaps that would be the right time to break and discuss whether these documents can be shown to the witness. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, all the -- we are aware of the fact that the Prosecution wasn't able to abide by your decision with regard to the new documents and provide them 24 hours in advance. For the sake of the transcript, I would like to say that although my mobile was on throughout the night, we did not receive any messages in the course of the night. We saw the documents five or six minutes [Realtime transcript read in error "months"] ago when they were given to us and for this reason I fully agree with the suggestions made by my learned friend, namely that we should first have a look at the documents and then hear from the Prosecution about the reason for which they want to use them and then we will state what our position is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Before I give the floor to the Prosecution again, as far as the new documents are concerned, as you know, we rendered an oral decision stating that new documents could only be used to check a witness's credibility or to refresh a witness's memory. These are the only two reasons for which we said that the documents that the Prosecution had after the end of the Prosecution's case could be used. They can be used either to test the credibility of a witness or to refresh a witness's memory. We also added that if the Prosecution wanted to use such material, we wanted these documents to be disclosed at least 24 hours in advance. Defence counsel examined the witness yesterday about certain issues not contained in the written summary, and as a result, the Prosecution only realised that these issues would be addressed yesterday afternoon. For this reason, it was difficult to respect the 24-hour notice since the problem arose yesterday afternoon. Defence counsel, Mr. Dixon, told us that as far as testing the witness's credibility is concerned, it would be best to wait to hear the questions and answers before using the documents, if necessary. It's not necessary to use them before since we will wait to see whether there are any new elements that arise. Yesterday the witness answered certain questions, and that is the situation we are in now. Is there anything that the Prosecution would like to say before the Judges discuss the issue? Yes, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the sake of the transcript, I would like to say that on page 4, 11 -- 10 and 11, instead of "five to six minutes," it says "five to six months." So I would be grateful if that could be changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This will be done. I will now give the floor back to the Prosecution. You have heard what the Defence has said, and I will now give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I'll try to be brief. I just want to say that the examination-in-chief was concluded -- of the witness Fehim Muratovic was concluded at around 4.00 yesterday afternoon, which is already within the 24-hour time frame. I personally was then leaving the courtroom and was approaching both Defence counsels and it is true I only exchanged with Mr. Rodney Dixon a mobile telephone number, and I called him at some point tonight when a selection of documents had not been done. I -- Mr. Dixon ensured to me that I could call late, and I indeed did so. And I did call Mr. Dixon this morning and gave him all the documents which have been selected, and this is actually the final selection. The two new documents which had been selected had been disclosed to the Defence. I will state the date and everything later. I can ensure, Your Honours, that these two documents relate to issues which have not been covered by the Defence summary which the Prosecution had received in advance of Mr. Muratovic's examination-in-chief. They relate exclusively to the guerrilla unit, and the fact that Mr. Muratovic would talk about the guerrilla unit was not known to the Prosecution prior to yesterday's examination-in-chief. So therefore, the Prosecution is aware about the 24-hour deadline and has tried to do its best by putting the Defence counsels on advance notice as much as possible. I was also, when I was coming in this morning, consulting with our case manager, Mr. Andres Vatter, and he told me though there was time available, there is at this late stage no possibility to store the documents into the usual facilities because at this late stage in the day, it would have been highly unlikely that the Defence counsels would have opened the disclosure box. So for this reason, the actual disclosure occurred, as was stated by my learned friends, in the courtroom. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges, having deliberated, we decided that when the credibility of a witness was at stake or refreshing a witness's memory was at stake, in such cases we could grant leave to present new documents. It would be best to start with the cross-examination, and we will see what the situation is as the witness provides his testimony. Although the document wasn't examined in detail by the Defence, they weren't in a position to do so, but nevertheless, I'm sure that given the fact that they are so professional, this will allow them to assess the situation. They will be able to assess the situation since they have the document. They've had it for a few minutes. I don't know whether the document is long or not, but if it's quite brief, they won't need a long time to assess the document and to be in a position to put pertinent questions since after the Prosecution has put its questions to the witness and after we've heard the witness's answers, you will have sufficient time for additional questions that relate to the document. Mr. Usher, could you call the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, you had to wait for a few minutes but there was an issue we had to deal with, a minor issue we had to deal with. We will now continue with your testimony, which should be completed today, rest assured. Without wasting any more time, I will give the floor to the Prosecution for their cross-examination. Mr. Neuner, you may take the floor. Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We have a few questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. We were focused on the Prosecution, and I had forgotten about you, but I'm glad to give you the floor. And in addition, you have additional time to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Muratovic. I'm going to ask you a few questions on behalf of Mr. Amir Kubura from the 7th Brigade. Sir, you said yesterday that you had certain problems from March and April 1993 onwards with - and these are your words - "small groups of foreign nationals." You referred to one group called the Turkish guerrilla and another group which you referred to as the El Mujahedin group; is that right? If you could just give a yes for the purposes of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Could you please confirm, sir, that from your investigations the members of these groups, the foreign nationals that you referred to, none of them were ever part of any brigade of the 3rd Corps of the Bosnian army, nor were they commanded by any brigade, including the 7th Muslim Brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Mr. Muratovic, you weren't here for the trial up until now, but Their Honours have in the course of the trial heard mention made of a guerrilla platoon that was part of the 7th Muslim Brigade. It is an Anti-Sabotage Platoon consisting of local Bosnian soldiers, and some documents have been referred to in that regard. I want to ask you, given your evidence yesterday, and just so there's no confusion for Their Honours, the Turkish guerrilla unit that you referred to, that has nothing to do with the guerrilla platoon in the 7th Brigade or any other guerrilla unit within the Bosnian army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The Turkish guerrilla group had absolutely no relation to the guerrilla or, rather, the unit that was also called guerrilla unit and was part of the 7th Muslim Brigade, as far as I know. The guerrilla group from the 7th Muslim brigade was composed of local people from Zenica and the surrounding villages and places. There was the town guerrilla and the mountain guerrilla, that's what they called themselves, and they had absolutely no connection with this guerrilla group that we have mostly been discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. Since Defence counsel has completed examination, I will now give the floor to the Prosecution for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Muratovic. My name is Matthias Neuner. I am appearing here along with my colleagues on behalf of the Prosecution. I will put a couple of questions to you, and the aim is not to confuse you, but if you don't understand a question, please ask me to repeat it or rephrase it and I will try to do so. Do you understand this?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In the military security organ of the 3rd Corps, you testified yesterday you started as a clerk. When exactly did you start your duties as a clerk, and at what point in time were you appointed to the post of assistant commander of counter-intelligence staff and security affairs? Please just state the dates.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said yesterday, the military security service of the 3rd Corps in the course of 1993, particularly in early 1993, was a service that was evolving. Formally we had an establishment within the unit. We had all the allocated posts, but most of us who worked there were not professionals by our qualification, so everybody did everything. I entered the service in mid-March 1993. Specifically, the counter-intelligence assistant, the post that I began, began in mid-August 1993. My colleague Osman Vlajcic was the assistant chief for counter-intelligence affairs. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I have to ask you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I started doing this job in July, not August.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Just to confirm again, in July 1993, you were no longer a clerk within the military security organ, but from July 1993 onwards, you were assistant commander of counter-intelligence staff and security affairs in the 3rd Corps organ for military security. Just say yes if it is so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there an interpretation problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not an interpretation problem, but my colleague is relying on the testimony of the witness or the statement of the witness, because the witness never said that in July of 1993 he left the service. He said that in the first quarter of 1994, he moved to the duty of deputy -- assistant commander for counter-intelligence. So we believe that a question which is actually not based on a previous answer by the witness is inadmissible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but the Prosecution has the right to put to the witness questions and to hear from him which duties he performed and exactly what he did. If there is any doubt about exactly what his duties were, then now is the proper time to clarify that. So I believe that the Prosecution has a right to ask these questions. I personally did not understand quite what exactly we're discussing here, but please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Let me start from scratch, from anew. Mr. Muratovic, you were a clerk from mid-March 1993 in the military security organ of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Until what time did you remain in that post?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the military security service practically until the end of the war in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What I'm trying to clarify is you said yesterday you were a clerk first and at some point in time you became, within the MS, military security organ of the 3rd Corps, at some point in time you were moving up to the position of assistant commander of counter-intelligence staff in security affairs. When were you no longer a clerk but when did you perform the new function as assistant commander of counter-intelligence? Just state a date, a point in time, please.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, all of the duties that I mentioned are as -- are within one of the organs. These are just separate parts of one and the same organ. In the beginning, I was a clerk for security within the organ, but in the beginning everybody did everything. All of us in the organ performed all of the duties in accordance with the specific orders from our superiors. However, later, in order to respect the establishment of classifications, we were allocated to certain posts. I cannot recall the exact dates, but what I'm saying is that in the first quarter of 1994, I was appointed to this post assistant commander for counter-intelligence affairs -- counter-intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And on that new post, from the first quarter of 1994 you remained throughout the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. And there was some other changes there, too. A long time has passed since then. There were many events. So at this point in time, especially under these circumstances, I'm not able to give you a specific answer about all the duties that I performed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand that, but can you just tell the Judges, did you stay in the military security organ of the 3rd Corps throughout the war, without giving the exact duties which you performed there?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I stayed in the security organ of the 3rd Corps, except for the last four or five months of the war when I moved to the post of chief for housing affairs of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: How many staff members were in the military security service of the 3rd Corps in March 1993 when you came? Just state a number.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, there weren't too many of us. I think there were perhaps four or five people at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you stated yesterday that with the arrival of Mr. Dugalic, Ramiz Dugalic, which was at about the same time, the number of staff increased. Until June 1993, approximately how many more members did join the staff?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to the military security service, there were two people dealing with security matters in that service and also a person who performed the duties of secretary in the organ. When I came, this number increased by three people. I can't really be precise. In June, there were three more people, so there were five of us at the most.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The military security organs from the brigades within the 3rd Corps area of responsibility, did they usually report to your 3rd Corps security -- military security organ or did they also bypass and send reports upwards to the military security administration of the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military hierarchy, the command and control system in the military is of a gradual nature. The organs from the lower units, from brigades and independent battalions, could not communicate directly with a command that was higher than the corps command. So they were directly in communication with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So if a military security organ of a brigade would assemble intelligence information, the exclusive channel to send this information upwards was the channel to your organ, the military security organ of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Let me turn now to Bugojno. On what day in mid-August 1993 did you go to Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it was on the 16th of August, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You testified yesterday, on page 28 and 29, that before you went there, and I quote you now: "The chief of security had previously been present there in Bugojno." Do you recall approximately how many days before you yourself went to Bugojno did Mr. Dugalic visit the town?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, this was perhaps two weeks before we went there. From ten days to two weeks, to 14 days. That was the time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Before Mr. Dugalic left for Bugojno, I understand at the beginning of -- approximately at the beginning of August 1993, did he tell you why he went there?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Dugalic was my superior officer, so he did not have to tell me why he was going to Bugojno. He did not have that obligation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand that. How long did he stay in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You said you were in Bugojno on the 15th of August -- excuse me, 16th of August, 1993. Who was the first person you met in -- once you arrived in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I came to Bugojno, it was logical that I would meet with my colleague in the local unit at the command of the 307th Brigade. So I met the assistant commander for security of that brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you, for the benefit of the record, state his name, please.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Enes Handzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you testified yesterday you spoke to somebody from the 307th Brigade. This is Mr. Enes Handzic? Just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did you speak to somebody else while you were in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was in Bugojno, I also had a meeting with a person from the Operations Group, Mr. Kemal Dzafic, the assistant commander for security. And we also tried to have a meeting with the commander of the municipal defence committee of Bugojno, Mr. Vlaho Jelic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: In the -- you testified at length about the conversation with the military -- with the -- with your colleague from the 307th Brigade. What did you discuss with Mr. Kemal Dzafic, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same topics that I discussed with Mr. Handzic I also covered with Mr. Kemal Dzafic; the current situation in Bugojno, the treatment of the prisoners, the possibility of transferring those persons to Zenica, to the POW centre. These were the questions that we talked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And what were you told by your colleague from the OG?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: His answers were the same as those by Mr. Handzic. He told me about the same problems regarding the transport of those individuals to Zenica. He briefly talked about the situation in the town of Bugojno, the situation with the prisoners of war in the places where they happened to be accommodated at that time, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What did he say about the situations of the prisoners of war in the temporary detention facilities in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What did he say? What did he tell you? Like everything was going fine or there were certain problems? You mentioned yesterday already something.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Mr. Enes Handzic and from Mr. Dzafic I got the same answers; that the prisoners of war were mostly doing fine except for this one incident where some members of the 307th Brigade whose families were killed by members of the HVO in the village of Vrbanja who broke into one of those centres which happened to be at the furniture salon. They attacked five or six members of the HVO. One of them was killed, died, and the others were given medical treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you recall from your conversations at about what point in time in August 1993 did this incident occur with the furniture salon? Was this briefly before you talked to them or did your colleagues tell you it was a week or two weeks before you talked to them?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that. It would be very difficult for me to tell you exactly when this happened, but it was before we arrived at Bugojno. I don't know how many days before our arrival it was, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Did they mention the name of any victims who had been beaten or of the person who died to you?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They told me the name of the person who died.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you still recall that name, please?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, I don't. But I mentioned that name in the report that I drafted once I returned from Bugojno. I did note down his name, but I really do not remember now what his name was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You said yesterday that upon your return to Zenica you sent this report to your superior. Is this Mr. Dugalic, just for clarification?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I went to Bugojno with my colleague, Mr. Dugalic happened to be sick, and he was at home recuperating. I addressed my report to the commander of the 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And did you ever receive a response from the commander of the 3rd Corps in relation to that incident?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never received a written response, but in a conversation that I had with him, the commander said that what we did up there was well done, that we did a good job.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I don't understand. You were reporting to Mr. Hadzihasanovic that a person had died and that people were beaten in the furniture salon. I don't understand why this can be considered a good job. Can you explain?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't understand each other. The thing that happened in the furniture salon was not a good thing, but it was a good thing that steps, legal steps, were taken against the persons who committed what they did against the members of the HVO, because those people who entered the furniture salon and beat up those HVO members were punished. The commander of the local unit and the assistant security commander took the appropriate legal steps vis-a-vis those persons in accordance with regulations of the 3rd Corps and in accordance with the competencies that they had out in the field. And that was to punish all forms of military disciplinary violations or any other criminal acts.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand you were told by your colleagues in Bugojno that such legal steps had been taken. Did you yourself verify that information by visiting the furniture salon, for example, or visiting the detained perpetrators or suspected perpetrators of the incident while you were in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: During my stay in Bugojno, I didn't go to any of the places where the POWs were held, but I also had no reason to doubt anything that my colleagues had told me. These were professionals, people who performed their jobs in a responsible way. So there was no need for me to check that. They had no reason to conceal anything or to lie in their reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Are you aware that a trial against these two perpetrators was ever conducted?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They were brought before the military disciplinary organ in Bugojno and were punished. That's what the report said that we received.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: When did you receive that report? About, approximately.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: We received an oral report when we were in Bugojno. At that time, we were told that the legal proceedings were under way and that these persons were in detention, in military detention in Bugojno, these two persons who beat up the members of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the potential perpetrators? Were you told these names but you have simply forgotten since it's so much time ago? Were you told while you were in Bugojno the names of the perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume that they told us what the names of those people were, but it didn't mean anything to me, so I really don't know what their names were.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand from your testimony in the last minutes that there was quite a frequent exchange about the military security situation in the temporary detention facilities in Bugojno or about the situation there between the military security service of the 307th Brigade and the 3rd Corps military security organ in August 1993. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: When we were there, of course we talked. When we went to Bugojno as well as during the visit of our chief to Bugojno, we talked to those people, and that's quite logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But after you went back to Zenica, you also received information about the situation in the temporary detention facilities in Bugojno, or did any information stop? I'm just asking you, did you receive reports, information?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: We would receive sporadic reports. They were not regular reports, but occasionally we did receive reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you my last question about Bugojno, about the transfer of detainees from temporary detention facilities in Bugojno. You said yesterday there was a convoy. Can you please state whether the convoy was finally at a later point in time reaching Zenica or whether only a few members from the detention facilities, the few members, detainees from this detention facilities did go to the KP Dom Zenica or can you state that no detainees from the detention facilities in Bugojno ever came to the KP Dom Zenica? Just to clarify.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The convoy did not leave Bugojno. And I mentioned several reasons for that. The vehicles were inoperative, then also the initiative by the local Croat intellectuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understood that, but my question was directed to since the convoy obviously did not reach Zenica, did at some later point in time detainees from the detention facility were transferred to Zenica, fewer detainees? That's my only question.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, the transfer never took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to talk now about the dual line of command in the -- or by the 3rd Corps organ for military security. You testified yesterday that when security threats occurred in the 3rd Corps area of responsibility, such a dual line of reporting by the 3rd Corps military security organ was in use; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The dual chain of command was not used only in such cases. The line of command in the military security service is dual regardless of the situation out in the field. We have expert command, and we have the command line, command -- chain of command, and that is how it is in peacetime and in wartime. That is how it is in our service and in all the military security services in all the countries of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So you informed the 3rd Corps Commander, and you informed the security administration of the Supreme Command, which was based in Sarajevo; right?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The military security administration was the expert organ which issued orders to us in the 3rd Corps. So without the permission of the security administration in the staff, we were not able to take any steps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If you wanted to relay information to the Supreme Command in the besieged town of Sarajevo in 1993, what technical means did you use to send reports, to send information there?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the building of the 3rd Corps Command, there was a communications centre. I am not a technical person, so I don't know how this was done, but I assume that this was done through radio communications and it would be an encrypted line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: As you just explained, such information would, one way or another, in encrypted form reach the Supreme Command in Sarajevo. Would you agree with me that certain information could go to Sarajevo but the transfer of troops from the besieged capital, for example to the 3rd Corps area of responsibility, was far more difficult at the time, if not impossible?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the beginning, in the course of 1993, transferring troops of any kind from Sarajevo was impossible and it wasn't done.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So would you, therefore, agree with me that in order to address security threats in the 3rd Corps area of responsibility, the 3rd Corps had to essentially rely on its own manpower?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the 3rd Corps, there were forces in the free territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Apart from the forces of the ABiH and the 3rd Corps and apart from the forces of the 1st Corps that were surrounded in Sarajevo, there were other forces in the territory, and there was the five -- the 5th Corps, the 6th Corps, the 1st Corps. So such communications weren't completely impossible. It was possible to transfer some forces from one area to another area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: But effectively, security threats occurring in your area of responsibility were primarily dealt with the available troops in the 3rd Corps area of responsibility. Isn't at that true?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Zenica and its surroundings from the very beginning of the aggression on our country until the last day when some sort of agreement was signed, there were permanent threats. Initially we only relied on our own forces in our area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just for the sake of the transcript, on page 21, line 11, after the word "staff" the words "the Supreme Command" are missing. That's what the witness said. It says "staff", but it doesn't mention the Supreme Command. The witness said "the Supreme Command Staff."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So you said, "Initially we only relied on our own forces in our area." From the perspective of the military security service, does this mean if you have intelligence information you as the military security service have an interest to apprise your commander with that information since he is in charge of forces to solve that security threat?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It should have been like that, but the security organ and the intelligence organ makes assumptions about the situation, which doesn't mean that these assumptions are fully correct, fully accurate. So they don't have to inform their commanders on all cases, because informing superiors about all such assumptions might just create confusion. I don't know if you have understood what I'm trying to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What I wanted to say is you had certainly an interest to solve security threats in your area of responsibility, and you collected information on how big, how small the threat was. And you also said that basically the available troops were those from the 3rd Corps area of responsibility. So my only question was did you inform the 3rd Corps commander, according to your own assessment, adequately in 1993 about security threats occurring in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have said, when I arrived in the organ at the beginning of 1993, I worked as an official. I was an official and informing the corps commander wasn't something that was done at my level. There were others who would be involved in such matters or who perhaps didn't act in this way, so I couldn't really answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to switch to the guerrilla. You testified to my learned colleague that the Turkish guerrilla unit was different from the guerrilla unit the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade. What do you know about the guerrilla units or groups within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't like there to be any confusion [Realtime transcript read in error "conclusion"]. The term "guerrilla" doesn't mean it was a guerrilla unit, not at all. At the beginning of the war, since the men had watched a lot of TV or films, they probably gave such names to their units, perhaps to have an effect on the other side. I don't know what the reason was, but that unit was not at all different from other units in the 3rd Corps. The guerrilla that was in the 7th Brigade was nowhere different from other units in the 3rd Corps. But in the case -- that was not the case for the Turkish guerrilla group which was composed of foreigners.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Could I just clarify something in the transcript before it goes off the page, and that is on page 24, line 4, the witness said, "Well, I wouldn't like there to be any confusion," not "conclusion." So if that could just be corrected. Sorry to interrupt. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you know who commanded the guerrilla -- I call it group now, the guerrilla group within the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade in 1993?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who commanded the so-called guerrilla group. That's not what I would call it. In any event, it was a man from that area, Zenica or the surroundings. I don't know exactly where he was from. But the men in that unit were local men from that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can we switch now to the so-called Turkish guerrilla. Was this Turkish guerrilla stationed in Zenica or where was it stationed?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Turkish guerrilla group was stationed in the nursery building. They broke into that building. It was in Travnicka Street, in Travnicka Street in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: According to the information you collected, this group had a leadership, you said. Was the leader of this group a person called Kemal Turcin or Kemal the Turk?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how he called himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What do you know about this Kemal Turcin?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given what I've heard about him, this was a criminal. He had committed certain crimes in the territory of Turkey, and at the beginning of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, he found refuge in Bosnia. He fled from the law in Turkey.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And about his activities on the ground in Zenica, do you know anything? What did he do in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, he and the entire group mostly committed illegal acts, not to say crimes. This involved trafficking goods, fuel, cigarettes, ammunition, weapons. Criminal acts. And in spreading panic among the population. So they were involved in black marketeering. They, in a certain sense, terrorised the civilian population in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you have any information whether this group was also stationed in Arnauti, or was in Arnauti another group stationed? This is a village about 12 kilometres east of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know exactly where the village is located but I don't know if the group were stationed in Arnauti. As far as I know, they were stationed in Travnicka Street in the nursery building and in a supermarket that was next to the nursery school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So you said you know that village and you don't think that this unit was stationed there. Which unit was stationed there in Arnauti? I'm referring to a unit of foreigners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. There is perhaps a translation error. I heard that this group was in a nursery school and in English I can see that it says a supermarket. So were they in a supermarket or in a nursery school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, in the nursery school and the building of the supermarket next to the nursery school. So they were in these two buildings. These were the two buildings they used and they were next to each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And where were they? Were they in the nursery school or in the supermarket?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the nursery school and the supermarket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In both these buildings. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Before I ask you the question about Arnauti, can you just state, please, how many people were in the Turkish guerrilla, according to your information?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were never able to establish the number exactly since these were mobile groups. Some of them were in that area, but they would circulate in the area, so I couldn't say how many men there were in that group.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You said also that at some point in time you arrested the entire leadership of this guerrilla group. Can you give the approximate date when you arrested or the military security service arrested the entire leadership? You said that on page 25 of yesterday's transcript.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday, towards the end of 1993 and at the beginning of 1994. Please don't insist on the exact date because I can't really remember the date. A lot of time has passed since then. But having monitored this group for a number of months, we asked the Supreme Command Staff or other security service to tell us what we should do with these people. We were told that they should either be placed under the control of the ABiH or that they should be arrested. Since they refused to be placed under the control of the ABiH, the 3rd Corps military police battalion took action and the leaders of that group were arrested. They were processed by the civilian organs. That was at the end of 1993 and at the beginning of 1994, more or less. And that is when that group ceased to exist in the territory of Zenica. The remaining men from that group were Bosniaks, and they had been in the group for certain benefits that they had received. People were starving in the area of Zenica at the time and they would receive flour, sugar, oil, et cetera. But these local men then joined the regular units of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You just said that "these local men joined the regular units of the ABiH." Do you have any recollection about how many local men, approximately how many local men you're talking about, and which ABiH units did they join?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know. I really don't know how many such men there were. But this included the 7th Muslim, the 314th, 303rd. Those were the units that were in the area of Zenica at the time, and they joined these units.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So the local men who were for a certain period of time in the Turkish guerrilla did stay in Zenica and joined the 303rd and probably, if you're talking about the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, you're talking, I assume, about the 2nd Battalion of the 7th Muslim Mountain Brigade, and the 314th, the battalion of the 314th, who was stationed in Zenica; is that correct? Just say yes --

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Did the military security service of the 3rd Corps ever receive any documents, any requests from this guerrilla unit in 1993? Did somebody from this unit approach the military security service of the 3rd Corps and ask for something, request something?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware that there were any requests made.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Were you personally, in 1993, dealing with the threat posed by this Turkish guerrilla or was a colleague of yours dealing -- within this military security organ dealing with the Turkish guerrilla? Who was the responsible person for the Turkish guerrilla within your service?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I recall, from the month of June 1993, the counter-intelligence jobs in the security service or the work with those foreigners was performed by my colleague, Osman Vlajcic. I don't know if they contacted him. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I want to talk a little bit about the Mujahedin unit, or first of all about the foreigners, the so-called Mujahedin. At the time you were arriving in mid-March 1993, what was the knowledge within your service, the military security organ of the 3rd Corps? What was the knowledge of this unit about this -- these people? Where were they based?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time, we practically had no information about these people. We knew that they were there in that area, moving around, that new people were appearing amongst them every day, but we didn't really know exactly what the situation was and nobody was entrusted with dealing with them or finding out what this was all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Who was the responsible person in your unit at the 3rd Corps military security service who from then on dealt with the problem of the -- problem -- with the Mujahedin? Did you deal with them or ...

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said in the beginning, from March 1993 to approximately June 1993, we all did everything. So we acted in accordance with tasks issued by superior commanders. From June 1993, we all received specific tasks and our own area of activity. So Mr. Vlajcic was in charge of the counter-intelligence within the organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You said yesterday - this is page 23, line 20 - "In April 1993, we sent an inquiry to the security administration of the Supreme Command in order to find out how to deal with the problem of the Mujahedin." What response did you receive -- or first of all, do you recall at what point in time did you send that request out? Was it the beginning of April or was it the end of April 1993, when the Supreme Command was contacted?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me clarify this first. When I say we sent out an inquiry, I'm talking on behalf of the organ. I did not personally do that. This was done by my superior commander. The inquiry was sent out in early April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And are you familiar with a response by the Supreme Command?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Supreme Command centre replied to the effect that we should try to find out who these persons were to try to identify them, to see where they were coming from and which channels they were using to get to Zenica, how many people there were, what were their intentions, in view of the fact that this was something that was completely unknown to us. They spoke a foreign language, we didn't know the people, we were not familiar with their customs; we simply didn't know anything about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And that reply, to the best of your recollection, came within a short period of time after your service had sent out the initial request or it took some time to get this response?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really am not able to respond to that question. I don't remember how much time passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You said yesterday at the beginning you couldn't get -- you tried to infiltrate these people - I'll just leave it there - but you basically didn't succeed at the beginning or you had problems with doing this. Are you aware that there were locals staying with this unit or locals staying with these people, local Bosnian people?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, this wasn't so. Later, when the unit stationed itself where it did, then the local population joined the unit. In my personal opinion, the reason why these people joined that unit was of a social or economic nature. As I said, these people who entered the Turkish guerrilla did that because of certain benefits. They received food from the unit. The same thing applied to this other unit, the El Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Mujahedin, that group of people. People joined them because of that reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You said earlier and later when they were stationed. Can you just inform the Trial Chamber what -- to approximately what time period are you referring by "earlier," and what do you mean by "later" when they were stationed? What time period are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning, when I say, I mean specifically when I joined the military security service in March 1992, you could already see them there in the streets, and you can see them moving around the town. When I say that they were stationed, then I'm talking about the autumn of 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So the comments, the last comments you made about the presence of these foreigners, you were talking about the presence of these foreigners in Zenica; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: It was March 1993 and not March 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. Page 31, line 9, it said 1992, but it should state 1993, March 1993. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You were talking yesterday on page 26 about the headquarter of the Mujahedin in Zenica. Was this building located on the premises of the company Vatrostalna in Podbrijezje or are you referring to another location?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean that place. I mean the administrative building of the Vatrostalna company in Podbrijezje. This is a suburb of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: If I may ask you, before these people, the Mujahedin, moved in, was this building used by or as a headquarter of the Frankopan Brigade, headed by Zivko Totic in early 1993, or was this another building?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command of the Jure Francetic HVO Brigade was in that building, but when these people came, these foreigners, the building was empty. It was abandoned. So they entered a building that was empty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: To the best of your recollection, when did the Jure Francetic Brigade abandon that building in 1993? Was it around the 8th June time period or earlier?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly, but I believe that it was in mid-1993. Probably in the month of June, but I don't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: According to your information, how many Mujahedin were moving into that building?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was practically impossible to establish. The numbers fluctuated continuously. They were not stationed in one place. In the beginning, they were in Mehurici, in the Bila valley, so that every day they would be going back and forth from there. It was very difficult to determine how many there were. We invested a lot of effort to try to establish exactly how many of them there were, but we were never successful in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Can you inform the Trial Chamber how far that building or headquarter in Podbrijezje was away from the 3rd Corps headquarter? How many kilometres, approximately?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Approximately ten to 12 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Were there any ABiH units stationed in Podbrijezje or was the -- were the Mujahedin the only force stationed in that part, in that suburb of Zenica?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there were no B and H army units there where the El Mujahedin group was, the one that had taken up that facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I didn't ask for the same premises but for Podbrijezje as such, for the suburb or -- how far, to your recollection, was the next ABiH unit away?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm thinking. It was the command of the 314th Brigade that was about eight to nine kilometres from that location.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: And you said yesterday that you tried to intercept telephone conversations. Were you referring to the intercepting of telephone conversations in Mehurici or were you referring to the intercepting of telephone conversations in Podbrijezje headquarter or both?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was thinking of the telephone calls from the command of the group, from -- in Podbrijezje.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: What was the outcome -- or when did the interception of telephone conversations start, approximately?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not able to say. I wasn't performing those duties at the time. This was already from June until the end of 1993, and that was already the area of responsibility of Mr. Vlajcic. Excuse me. Can I add something else?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the application of methods and means of the military security service. So this is something that is secret. And the application of these methods is something that only the person actually working on that task would be familiar with, because if more people knew about it, there would be the danger that the attempt to acquire information in this way would fail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I appreciate that explanation. Did you perform any -- were you involved in any surveillance, in any counter-intelligence relating to this group? Was this also part of your tasks?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not involved in any tasks like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: My last question is you said you stayed throughout the war in the 3rd Corps area of responsibility. Are you aware that at the end of the war an order was given by the Supreme Command to -- with regard to the documentation or the dissembling of documentation about this group and that this documentation should be handed over to a committee of the 3rd Corps? Are you familiar with any such order? I'm referring to the time period December 1995 now.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not familiar with that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: At this point in time, the Prosecution has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It's half past 10.00. We will have our technical break and we will resume at about five to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume, and I will give the floor to the Defence for re-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have a few questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Muratovic.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My learned friend asked you whether, after you had filed a report on the visit to Bugojno, you had any contact with the commander and you said that your chief was ill at the time and that you sent that to the commander. Could you tell me, within your security service in the 3rd Corps, who usually contacted the commander?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the 3rd corps security service, my chief, my superior officer alone had contact with the commander.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Given the fact that he was ill, was the fact that you contacted him an exception? Was this a rule? Is this how the members of the service would communicate with the commander?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when I contacted the commander, this was an exceptional circumstance, but since we had assessed -- since the report on Bugojno on the situation of the POWs was such, this is how we decided to proceed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When your chief returned from sick leave, who continued to have contact with the commander as of that date?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only my chief did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were in the security organ of the 3rd Corps. You said that there were security organs up to the level of battalions. Whose duty was it primarily, whose responsibility was it if they found out that ABiH members had committed a crime of any kind to investigate the matter and to institute proceedings against the perpetrators if the perpetrators were identified?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the organ's duty to report on such events if it happened in the zone of responsibility. It was the duty from the organ of that battalion. And this information is then forwarded to the corps security organ and then we propose further measures to be taken.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you obtain information, when you -- when you obtain information through investigating the situation on the site and to determine that the relevant organ from a subordinate unit took all measures that it should have taken in accordance with the law and the orders issued, when you determine that that is the case, is it necessary for you to check what was subsequently done or is this something that is the responsibility of the organ in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the organ in the unit concerned that is involved in the matter, and I really don't see why we should have to check anything in the service, because the organs in those subordinate units would have no role in that case. There would only be an organ in the corps or the Supreme Command that would be involved in those matters. If we had any doubts as to the work of the organs in subordinate units, this is what the situation would be like.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that in June there were about five of you in the 3rd Corps security organ. I assume that this organ developed and that there were more members towards the end of the year, but even if there were -- or if there had been three times as many of you, would you have been in a position to check on all the criminal proceedings instituted against ABiH members throughout the territory of the 3rd Corps? Would this have had a purpose and would it have at all been possible?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if we had a look at the number of criminal reports filed or the number of proceedings instituted and compared that to the number of people working in the 3rd Corps security organ, this would have been impossible to do, especially when the roads were blocked, territory was cut off and enemy lines were in the vicinity.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muratovic, you mentioned the chain of command, and you [Realtime transcript read in error "I"] mentioned the expert line which meant that you had to provide information on all measures taken, and you also mentioned the line of command responsibility. My learned friend asked you about the possibility of troops or units leaving Sarajevo that had been encircled and going to other areas. In your opinion, was there the possibility of the units leaving Sarajevo, and did this affect the line of command in the 3rd Corps and any other units?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This has no effect. I'm not sure I've really understood what you are asking me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Even though ABiH units which were deployed in Sarajevo that had been encircled, even though those units couldn't leave, did this in any way affect your responsibility to provide the security administration of the Supreme Command with information that you obtained?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We had this responsibility and this duty wasn't diminished, and we acted in accordance with our responsibilities. As far as all the events in our zone of responsibility are concerned, we provide the Supreme Command Staff security administration of all such information, and we requested that they provide us with instructions for further action.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did the blockade of Sarajevo in any way change the responsibility you had to follow the instructions that the security administration gave you with regard to how you should act after you had obtained information of interest to security or, rather, after you had obtained information about crimes committed?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The blockade of Sarajevo in no way affected the duty we had to inform on everything that happened in our territory.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There's a mistake in the transcript. 37, page 37, line 9. The word "I" appears instead of "you." I apologise for interrupting you. Given that dual line of command and whether there was a blockade or not, were you able to provide the corps commander with information gathered in the security organ, information that you had to forward to the security administration?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't provide all the information we obtained. The methods of the security service was not something that we communicated fully to the 3rd Corps, because if we had provided them with all the information we had, this could have been counter-productive and certain measures might have been taken that would not have been appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So that I'm quite clear about this, when you carried out your work, would you, for example, also be involved with members of the commands of subordinate units or the commander of the corps? Could they also be processed by your organ if you believed that this was necessary?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was part of the field of the work of the security service. They also had to control the command officers, and certain proceedings had also been instituted against high level officers in the ABiH, against brigade commanders, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To be quite clear about this, you said that this might create confusion and that certain measures might be taken. If you provided all such information to the commander, would the work that you did have any purpose?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I only have one more question for you which has to do with your response. You said that you had arrested the leaders of Turkish guerrilla group and you said that the Bosnians that were with them were assigned to other units. Tell me, if there were any doubts, if there was suspicion that these Bosnians had also committed crimes, were measures taken against them or were they granted an amnesty if you suspected that they had committed crimes?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the orders we received from the 3rd Corps Commander stated that the law was the same for everyone, for our local people and for foreigners who committed crimes. I could provide you with hundreds of examples when our people -- when people were starving in Zenica and in the free territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, wherever the ABiH was present, I can provide you with examples where people were held to account for having stolen ten kilogrammes of flour. Disciplinary measures taken against them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Muratovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We have no questions arising from the cross-examination by the Prosecution. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as I'm concerned. I have a few questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all with regard to the two guerrilla groups, in the sense brigade, in response to a question put to you by Defence counsel, you said that these groups were composed of people from the town or of men from the mountain. As far as you know, because apparently you are a counter-intelligence specialist, as far as you know, these men who were in the guerrilla groups, did they have uniforms or not?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course they had uniforms to the extent that this was possible for us. It was at the beginning of the war, 1992 and 1993. I don't know how you see the ABiH in that period, but to the extent that it was possible, the men wore uniforms that they had been given by the units or that they had obtained in some other way.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: These weren't guerrillas. It was a unit just like any other unit. It could have been called some sort of a company or a battalion, or they could have given them a name such as El Mujahedin, but these men were local men. There were no foreigners. The commander was a local man, and all the men were from the territory of Zenica or from the surrounding places. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Thank you. Very well. They had uniforms. In relation to the battalion or platoon, what was their specific mission when compared to other units? Did they have a specific mission which would have justified the use of the term "guerrilla"?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, on the whole the tasks they had were the same, but since these men were quite courageous, so to say, they were volunteers that the commander could always rely on when it was necessary to go into action or to oppose enemy action. Well, these men were, after all, courageous men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that they were courageous men, and they must have had particular missions to accomplish. Does that mean that these were high-risk missions, and were these missions that were to be carried out in the enemy's depth?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the time, all the tasks were risky tasks. As to tasks in the depth of enemy territory, I couldn't really say anything about that. I didn't have such information at my level that these were high-risk tasks. If the enemy penetrated the line, these were the men who would first mount a defence of the free territory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I'm following what you are saying, when there was an operation, an attack, let's say, they were at the front line.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness's answer was not audible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you certain of that?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sure of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll move on to another subject now. You spoke about two groups, the Turkish guerrilla group and the Mujahedin group. At the very beginning, perhaps there was some translation errors, but I noted this down: "We infiltrated our men in the Turkish guerrilla group," and then when the Prosecution put questions to you, you said that you tried to infiltrate men into the group. Could you be clear and solve this ambiguity. Had your service infiltrated the Turkish guerrilla group or did you try to infiltrate your men in the guerrilla group? Can you see the difference?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see the difference. I said that, and I was not talking about men from the service but people who worked for the service. I said that we managed to infiltrate our associates into the Turkish guerrilla group and we tried to infiltrate them in the other El Mujahid group and we were not successful in doing so. We tried to infiltrate them in the other group. Towards the end of autumn, because we had infiltrated our men into this first group, the leaders were arrested as a result of this action and this group then eased to exist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I'm following you correctly, does this mean that the infiltration into the guerrilla group resulted in success?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And does that mean, if I have understood you correctly, that at one point in time there were within the guerrilla group Bosniaks who had close contact with you and they could participate in various actions with the Turkish guerrilla group, and given the methods that you were applying, you were aware of what was happening.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Turkish guerrilla group couldn't have been used for the needs of the ABiH since they didn't want to place themselves under the control of the army. But through these men we found out what their intentions were. We obtained the information we needed in order to deal with the group. We found out about their strength, the weapons they had, about the areas they were deployed, about the accommodation used by the leaders, about the location of their flats, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're saying that thanks to the fact that men had infiltrated them, you knew about their strength, the weapons they had, about the accommodation they used, et cetera. In response to a question from the Prosecution who asked you how many of them there were, you weren't able to provide with us a number and now I see that you're saying that you knew how many of them there were. So how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how many there were. I'm still standing by what I said that we don't know how many there were. The approximate number of the Turkish guerrilla members was known but not for this other group, El Mujahedin. We never managed to establish exactly how many of them there were in spite of all our efforts and insistence to find out.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Very well. As far as the Turkish guerrilla group is concerned - I'm not talking about the Mujahedin right now, I'm talking about the Turkish guerrilla group - how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know. In response to a question, you said the end of 1993, beginning of 1994, you were given two possibilities; either to place them under control or to arrest them. That's page 27, line 11. Can you confirm that at your level or at the level of ABiH, at the level of the 3rd Corps, the issue of these members of the Turkish guerrilla or the Mujahedin resulted in the idea that they should either be placed under control or arrested. Could you clarify this matter.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the level of the security service of the 3rd Corps, an inquiry was sent to the B and H army Supreme Command security services administration about what to do about these people since they were creating problems in the town both for civilians as well as for the reputation of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. People, when they saw somebody in uniform, they would think that they were members of the army of B and H but they were in fact not members of the B and H army. After a certain period of time, I don't know exactly after how long, we received a response that they needed to decide whether they would place themselves under the control of the 3rd Corps or the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina or whether they needed to be dealt with, whether they had to be arrested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And my final question: You said that they were tarnishing the reputation of the army given their conduct and that they really presented you with a problem, and you have already said that these members of the Turkish guerrilla group committed crimes.
