I'm quoting you. You mentioned trafficking, black-marketeering, trafficking in weapons, spreading panic among the population, et cetera, terrorising the population, et cetera. You described what these men did. How can you reconcile the fact that there were men who committed crimes and later you placed them in the army or you wanted to put them under the control of the army? Could you clarify this issue. If you can't, just say that the question is too complicated and that you can't answer it. I'll repeat the question. You said that these men committed crimes and then it was necessary to solve the problem by making them join the army. One could come to the conclusion that the army was going to have delinquents among its troops. How would you explain this?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understood the question. I understand what you're saying. Placing them under the control, this group, the Turkish guerrilla group, I don't know how many people there were, perhaps there were 50 or 100, I said that the majority of the group comprised of Bosniaks, people who were there for purely economic reasons, for social reasons, in order -- they were there because they were receiving food. All of these people are innocent. All the Bosniaks did not violate the law. However, their complete leadership, the leadership of the unit, it turned out that these were some ten people, I'm not sure exactly how many there were, it's clear that by placing them under the control, they would be then subject to the laws and then they would have had to be processed for their deeds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As we don't have much time, I have one last question for you. You have just said that in this group there were innocent Bosnians who had to be put on the right path, in a certain sense, and you said that they had not done anything. You said that it was only the leaders. Shouldn't these Bosnians, as far as you know, given the fact that a state of war had been declared, shouldn't these Bosnians had been in army units? How is it that they were not in the army since there was a decree law according to which anyone fit for military service would be automatically mobilised into the army? Could you clarify this for us.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 3rd Corps had over 30.000 members, people who were mobilised, and it's clear that in the territory of about some 2 to 300.000 people - this was a joint territory - it's clear that you would have some 50 or 100 people who would try to evade their mobilisation duty and join other groups. In the beginning, this was easier because they simply concealed themselves inside these groups.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know - and this is my last question - when the leaders of the Turkish group were arrested, the Bosnians who were with them, were they assigned to units?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The majority passed into the composition of the 303rd, 314th, and the 7th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Very well. Does the Prosecution have any questions that arise from the Judge's questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You stated again that you didn't know the numbers of foreigners in the Mujahedin unit, the exact numbers. Are you aware that already in 1993 there were some lists of members of the so-called El Mujahedin detachment and that such lists contained up to nearly 190 names? I'm referring to foreigners as well as local names. Are you aware whether any such lists were existing in 1993?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: So you will therefore probably also not know that such lists contained a kind of letterhead, 3rd Corps, and stating basically -- mentioning the 3rd Corps on top of such lists? You don't have such information?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness said he doesn't know, so it's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Residovic, you would like to make an objection, but the document has been admitted as an exhibit. I did not specifically question the witness about Mujahedin. I put to him one question about their numbers, and he said that he didn't know. The Prosecutor would like to go a little further and is asking him whether he's aware of a list existing. Is that your objection or is this a tactical objection? I would like to know what this is about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is not a tactical objection. I just would like to say that the witness said that he didn't know that there was any such list, and after such a response, you cannot put additional questions about a list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. He said that he doesn't know about the list and he doesn't know their number.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Turning to the guerrillas, you said you didn't know the numbers of the Turkish guerrilla group. On the other hand side you said you infiltrated this group. You found out -- let's say the military security service of the 3rd Corps infiltrated this group. The military security service found out about where the commander was accommodated, how many weapons, that the majority of the members were local Bosnian members. If you have all these details available in the military security service, wouldn't that imply that the military security service was also aware about the absolute numbers of these people? If you know details about the apartments or about the accommodation of the leadership, then before you get such details, and if you have members in this unit infiltrating the unit, you will know how many members are in this unit or not.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not ruling out the possibility that somebody knew how many there were. I personally did not know how many of them there were. I didn't know how many members there were in the Turkish guerrilla.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I understand that. You talk about the supermarket or nursery being a kind of accommodation for the command or -- was this actually the accommodation of the command or was this the accommodation of the whole unit? Were these a kind of barracks or -- can you please explain?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't ask any questions about the supermarket or about the nursery school. I asked him to provide a more precise answer awhile ago, but in my direct questions that I put to the witness just a minute ago, this is not an issue that I raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Presiding Judge was asking you questions relating to operations, combat operations, of this Turkish guerrilla group. To the best of your recollection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I didn't ask any questions about the combat operations led by the Turkish group. I asked a question about the guerrilla group that was part of the 7th Brigade. I don't want this to be confused, otherwise Defence will be on their feet to object. My question was about the guerrilla and the 7th Brigade, not about the Turks. I wanted to state that in order to avoid having the Defence object, which would have resulted in a waste of time. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Thank you for this clarification. So I withdraw that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Turkish -- you said that you talked about the local members of the -- within the Turkish guerrilla, and you said that they were innocent, so to speak. How did you personally know that these local members within the Turkish guerrilla did not violate the law? On what basis do you say they are innocent?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Members of the Turkish guerrilla could be seen around town, and it was more or less known who committed these illegal acts, who was doing the smuggling, reselling fuel, who was intimidating the civilian population. This was something that the local people did not participate in.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: You said the law was the same for everyone. So it was applied for local people and for foreigners. Did you personally, with the work of the military security service of the 3rd Corps, come to the stage that the law was also applied against the Turkish, the leadership of the Turkish guerrilla? Were any legal proceedings instituted?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were handed over to civilian organs, and I don't know what happened to them after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Do you know what charges or what criminal reports were filed by the military security service of the 3rd Corps organ in relation to the Turkish guerrilla?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were not members of the army, and military security did not issue charges against them. They were handed over to the civilian organs who then dealt with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: I wasn't asking for charges. I was asking for criminal reports to be filed by the military security service of the 3rd Corps. Since you had infiltrated the group, you had knowledge -- you had gained knowledge about the group, were some criminal reports filed, to your knowledge? Or maybe there weren't any filed.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Like I said, they were handed over to the civilian bodies, to the civilian judiciary bodies, and they then dealt with them further.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: Along this line I just want to ask if foreigners are stationed in the 3rd Corps area of responsibility and you in the military security service received reports about potential crimes committed by foreigners, so brigade or military security services of brigades are sending reports upwards to the military security service ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: My learned friend has asked questions regarding this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I've heard a few questions now and I was paying careful attention to your questions and what the Prosecution has now asked about brigades, about prosecuting individuals, et cetera, has nothing to do with the questions that you put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Neuner. I didn't ask any questions about this. He answered a previous question and said that when these people were arrested, they were transferred -- or they were handed over to the civilian police who dealt with them, and I believe that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. he has answered the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NEUNER
utterances.text: The Prosecution has no further questions. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Muratovic, you said that for several months you surveilled this Turkish guerrilla group before you submitted an inquiry to the military security administration about taking further measures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: We first sent an inquiry to the administration asking them what to do. They instructed us to take certain steps which we did vis-a-vis these individuals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After you monitored this group, infiltrated it, and when you found out certain things, after that did you ask the military security administration about what you were supposed to do? When you provided them information about their numbers, the command cadre, actions and so on.

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the expert sense, the military security administration organ is superior to us, so everything that we did in relation to anyone else within the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps was something that we had to have permission for from the administration of the military security service of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You've already told us what kind of information you received and how you found out what was necessary. Were you able to ask for permission for an operation before you found out everything that you received back from your associates or information you got through other methods? Before you compiled all of this information were you able to embark upon an operation which you eventually carried out?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Theoretically we could have asked for that, but it wouldn't have made any sense. Only after we had compiled all of the information through different means could we then embark on the operation itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I assume we had some -- you had some kind of plan. I'm not sure how you do that in the security services. So who had to approve your plan of activity in relation to the guerrilla or anyone else that you were planning to take steps against?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: The chief of the security service administration of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Only one small follow-up clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I think you have made this clear already, but just so we can all be sure. Could you confirm that it was common throughout the Bosnian army for various brigades to have specialised units within those brigades that would perform specialised tasks on the front lines, such as doing reconnaissance work or anti-sabotage work, and that those units had different names depending on the brigade. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the practice. Those units were usually called manoeuvering units, and they were of that type. And these were units which were always prepared to combat certain enemy activities. Such a unit in the 7th Muslim Brigade was called like that. It was called guerrilla. At that point in time it seemed like a good idea to the people who were in that specialised unit to call themselves that, and that is what they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: And it would be correct, then, that there were other similar units in other brigades with different names performing the same kind of tasks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FEHIM MURATOVIC: [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, this concludes your testimony. Thank you for having come to The Hague, and thank you for having answered the questions put to you by the Defence, by the Prosecution, and by myself. On behalf of the Chamber, I wish you a good trip home and all the best in your career in the ministry where you work. I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll be calling the second witness into the courtroom. The Defence said that they needed 30 minutes yesterday. We'd best make sure that the witness doesn't have to stay over the weekend. Perhaps we will be able to complete this witness's testimony by 1.45 p.m. Mr. Registrar, we're in courtroom II, and I've noticed that courtroom III is available. Why are we in courtroom II since courtroom III is available? I'm taking this opportunity to put this question to you. Very well. Technical measures are being taken in courtroom III. This is why we could not use it. But we'll be in courtroom III next week. Mr. Registrar, I hope that the usher is aware of the fact that he should bring the second witness into the courtroom. Do you have any news?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. I would first like to make sure that you are receiving the interpretation of what I'm saying into your own language. Please say that you hear me and understand me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hear you and understand you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have been called here as a witness for the Defence to testify about certain events that you may have been familiar with in 1992 and 1993. Before you take the solemn declaration, I would be grateful if you could tell me your first and last names, your date of birth and place of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Ragib Hadzic. I was born on the 6th of July, 1950, in Vlasenica, in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you currently employed, and if so, what is your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a private business. I am a private --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. In 1992 and 1993, did you hold a position of any kind; and if so, what was your position and for which legal body did you work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked for the municipal prosecutor's office in Zenica and in the higher court or, rather, later in the cantonal court in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Have you already testified before an international or national court about the events in your country in 1992 and 1993 or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please read out the solemn declaration that the usher will show you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt at this point, but the witness said, and it's recorded like that, that his name was Mr. Ragib Hadzic and not Hodzic, but I may be wrong, because in the 65 ter summary it says Hodzic, and that plays a big role in our searches. I'm just wondering whether the Defence could clarify because then we could make some correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll ask the witness to spell his name. Could you please spell your name for us and that will clarify the issue immediately.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a mistake that is often made. My name is Hadzic, the second letter in my surname is A.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So in your passport or on your identity card your name is spelt with an H and A and not with an O; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Defence wrote your name with an O.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A mistake was obviously made. We didn't check it. It's correct to say that Mr. Hadzic worked in the prosecutor's office and he will only be talking about one subject that relates to Dusina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This could have caused problems for the Prosecution when searching electronically for information because HO wouldn't have yielded the same result as HA. So you have been called here as a witness for the Defence and I would like to provide you with some information about the procedure that will be followed here. You will first have to answer the questions put to you by the Defence, and they will be conducting what we call the examination-in-chief. Once this stage has been completed, which should not take more than 30 minutes, the Prosecution, who are to your right, will conduct what we call their cross-examination. The questions put to you in the course of the cross-examination must relate to the questions put to you in the course of the examination-in-chief. The difference between these two systems is that in the course of the examination-in-chief you must not be asked leading questions. On the other hand, the Prosecution is allowed to put leading questions to you. As you can see, matters become complicated here. After this stage has been completed, Defence counsel may ask you additional questions that relate to the questions put to you by the Prosecution. The three Judges who are sitting before you may also ask you questions at any point in time if they believe that it is necessary, but as a rule the Judges prefer to work for the -- wait for the parties to have completed their examination before intervening. As a rule, when the Judges ask questions, the purpose of our questions is either to clarify witness's answers or because we believe it is in the interest of justice to fill some of the gaps we have noted in the questions or in the answers. When the Judges ask questions -- after the Judges have asked questions, the parties have the right to ask the witness additional questions. Defence counsel will be the last to take the floor and they may put any questions they believe necessary to a witness after the Judges have put their questions to the witness. I would also like to point out that as you have taken the solemn declaration, this excludes the possibility of giving false testimony. And secondly, there is a provision that is applicable in this system and perhaps in certain other countries, when a witness answers a question, if the witness believes that his answer could be used at a subsequent date against him, in such a case the witness may refuse to answer the question. If this happens, but this is very exceptional and we have never had such a case to date, if this happens, the Chamber can compel the witness to answer the question but the witness is granted a form of immunity. This is a very specific measure. Without wasting any more time, I will now give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you hear my question, I would like you to pause slightly so that my question could be interpreted. I will also do the same thing when I hear your response, and in that way Their Honours and our learned friends in the courtroom can follow what you are saying. Did you understand me?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me what your qualifications are.

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: I completed the Faculty of Law in Sarajevo in 1975.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You told the Presiding Judge that you worked during the war --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was this in 1975 or 1985? We're not sure. We heard 1985 but the transcript says 1975.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The transcript has it right. I graduated on the 26th of November in 1975 in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you worked in the basic court and then you worked in the superior and then in the cantonal prosecutor's office of Zenica. Could you please tell us whether at some point during the war you stopped working in the prosecutor's office and worked in other duties. And if this happened, could you please tell us, how long were you away from the prosecutor's office during the war?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did have a short break when I was mobilised and sent for work duty. I performed the task of director of the centre for the Institute for the Investigation of Crimes Against Humanity and International Law, and this lasted from the summer of 1993 until April 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you spent a large amount of time in the prosecutor's office, could you please tell me what was the area covered by the higher prosecutor's office in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: According to the pre-war organisation of the judicial services in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the superior prosecutor's office and the superior court covered the municipalities of Zenica, Kakanj, Zavidovici, Zepca, Travnik, Vitez, Busovaca, Gornji Vakuf, Donji Vakuf, Bugojno, and Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell me, the superior prosecutor's office, was that responsible for the prosecution of persons for all criminal acts or were its jurisdictions connected to the gravity of those crimes?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: According to the general regulations, the superior prosecutor's office prosecuted persons who committed crimes for -- which were to be punished up to ten years in prison. And then the higher such bodies prosecuted persons who had committed crimes punishable by sentences of over ten years.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, who was the prosecutor in the high -- in the superior prosecutor's office?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: When I took upon -- that duty took upon myself, up to June 1997, the superior public prosecutor was Sulejman Kapetanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you were working in the prosecutor's office, what were the regulations that you applied in your work?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Up until 1978, we applied the Law on Criminal Procedure of the former SFRY, which was taken over as the republican law of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992 by a decree of the Presidency. The criminal law of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the general parts of the criminal law of the former SFRY, which were also applied to -- as republican law. And also we applied other regulations from the law of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, we would just like to clarify one thing which is in the transcript here. Perhaps it's just a misstatement. Can you please tell us up until when this Law on Criminal Procedure was applied.

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Up until the Law on Criminal Procedure of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And when was this?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: This was in 1998. I apologise. I made a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My colleagues are warning me. I would like to repeat some questions because the competency of the basic and the higher prosecutor's office remained a little bit unclear. So could you please tell me now, what was the basic prosecutor's office responsible for and for which acts was the higher prosecutor's office responsible? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: The criteria was the sentence. The basic prosecutor's office prosecuted persons which could be sentenced up to ten years of imprisonment. The higher prosecutor's office prosecuted persons for more serious crimes, punishable by ten years or more.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, during the war could you please tell me the basic and the higher prosecutor's office, who was under their jurisdiction?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: They had jurisdiction over civilians and over military persons only if they committed criminal acts in some kind of collusion or jointly with civilians.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, do you know whether, besides these prosecutors' offices, the basic and the superior offices in the area of Zenica and a broader area, was there any other prosecutor's office that was active; and if so, what were their jurisdictions?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: During the war there was also the district military prosecutor's office which was responsible to the military court in Zenica, and its jurisdiction included only military personnel and only civilians for very specific crimes. As far as I recall, we are talking about criminal acts committed against the arms -- armed forces in such cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order to use the fact that you worked in the prosecutor's office and on that basis so that we could find out a little more about the role of the prosecutor, could you please tell me when and based on what did the prosecutor, in accordance with our regulations, issue or initiate proceedings? Based on what information would he be able to start acting in accordance with the law?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: The prosecutor initiated criminal proceedings based on formal criminal charges, an act, a document that somebody, most often it would be the police, informed them that something had been committed that could be a criminal act. They could also initiate formal proceedings based on information received from some other sources. This was defined by law in such a way by saying that the prosecutor had been informed that a crime had been committed. This means that there were two possibilities based on which the prosecutor would assess the grounds for initiating criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Let's start from this second option. Could you please tell us what was the role or the responsibility of the prosecutor when he had been informed or when he learned information about indications existing of a criminal act being committed. What was then the prosecutor duty bound to do?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: He was obliged to check the grounds for the information that he received, which means that he was obliged to determine, according to law, the authenticity and reliability of the facts and information that he had learned. This was usually done through the organs for internal affairs. The received information was checked and specific orders were given to the interior -- the service for internal affairs. They were told who they were supposed to interview, possibly which cases or items they needed to deal with, and then after that this list would be completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If the prosecutor received a formal criminal charge, what were his duties and what was the procedure that he followed in such a case?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: If the material that came along with the criminal charges provided sufficient grounds for the prosecutor to conclude that there was reason to believe that a criminal act had been committed, then the prosecutor launched an investigation. He would formalise the charges, which under that law was called a request to conduct an inquiry. He would pass that on to the investigative judge and specify, first of all, the act constituting a criminal act, would provide his opinion of the legal qualification, and then he would instruct the investigative judge what actions he needed to take, and then at the end of the investigation he would decide to prosecute or not. If the material was not of sufficient quality to provide enough grounds for reasonable grounds to believe that a crime had been committed, then the prosecutor was obliged to complete that, to complete the missing facts or materials which would then be sufficient for reasonable grounds to believe, or he would conclude that there were no grounds to believe that a criminal act had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: What would the prosecutor do once he received formal criminal charges, which as you say would not indicate that there were reasonable grounds, or when the assembled material did not indicate that there was sufficient grounds to believe that a criminal act would be -- had been committed, what would the prosecutor then do with all of these documents, this material?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: If after the material was checked the material did not indicate that a criminal act had been declared, then in case of charges, a formal decision, a formal act would be adopted rejecting the criminal charges. There was specific reasons based on which you could reject criminal charges. If we're talking about the second option that we discussed, that the prosecutor had learned or found out through informal channels about a criminal act possibly be committed, then this would simply be filed. The material would be filed and the case would be considered closed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If the prosecutor assessed that the material at his disposal, given to him by the police, from a court or from the plaintiff did not point to a criminal act being committed and the prosecutor noted that by filing the material or rejecting the charges, in that case would this be a legally binding decision about a certain incident or event, or would the prosecutor have the option to review the case once additional evidence had been submitted?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. A formal ruling to reject the criminal charges would be the act of one side in the proceedings. And it doesn't have the res judicata or power. It doesn't have the power of a matter having been ruled upon. Each new fact or piece of evidence indicating the contrary from the conviction of the prosecutor would then be sufficient to continue proceedings in that case under legal procedures in force. After a case was filed, which we kept a record of through a general kind of ledger, it would in that case also be enough to hear of a new fact or for some new evidence to come so that this case could then again be reopened.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, could you please tell me who, according to our law, handled the overall pre-trial procedure?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: The pre-trial procedure was exclusively handled by the prosecutor, and it was his responsibility entirely.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When the prosecutor requested that an investigation be carried out and an investigative judge accepted this by a decision, who would then be in charge of handling the formal proceedings?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: The law on criminal proceedings of Bosnia and Herzegovina from 1978 was based on a judicial inquiry. So after the ruling to carry out an investigation was carried and then all the responsibility for that case would be borne by the investigative judge or by the court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you told us all the different places where you worked, you said that you had moved to the superior prosecutor's office and then to the cantonal prosecutor's office. What would be the competence of the Zenica cantonal prosecutor's office, and when was this office established?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: The Zenica cantonal prosecutor's office was established in 1997 when cantons were formed as special administrative units within the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina based on the constitution of the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. These prosecutor's offices inherited the jurisdiction of the former higher prosecutor's office. Then there was some newly formed municipalities, Jug, Tesanj, Maglaj, Zavidovici, Zepca, Zenica, Kakanj, Breza, Visoko, Olovo, and I think that that is all. This was all part of the canton.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When this canton prosecutor's office was formed, were there any military prosecutor's offices in existence at the time? What happened to them?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: The organs of the military judiciary, the military prosecutor's office and the military courts were abolished when the war ended, when the immediate threat of war had ceased, and all the organs of the district military prosecutor's office and the military courts became part of the higher cantonal -- Zenica canton prosecutor's office and the higher court.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, when you said that if a prosecutor found out some new facts or received some new material he would be able to review a certain case on which he had already ruled upon earlier or which was ruled upon by some other prosecutor who was evaluating that material. Could you please tell us whether you personally were ever in a situation where you had to reassess a decision of a colleague of yours in a case where there was not enough grounds to believe that a criminal act had been committed?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Not only did I review the decisions, my own decisions, but also the decisions of colleagues whose cases I had inherited. This was nothing unusual or new. It is quite normal that if some new fact or circumstance surfaces, to continue the criminal proceedings, because the basic procedure of work of the prosecutor's office in Bosnia and Herzegovina is consistency, because the prosecutor is obliged to carry out criminal proceedings in any situation where he had a sufficient quantity of evidence pointing to a criminal act being committed. So for us, these were guidelines in the prosecutor's office which were not debatable.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, tell me whether among those cases there was a case from January 1993 which concerned the events in Dusina.

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, there was such a case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me how and for what reason were you in a position to reassess decisions taken by your colleague from 1993?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: When the trial of General Blaskic commenced before this Tribunal, there was speculation among the public that a crime had been committed against the civilians in Dusina and that prisoners had been killed, that human shields had been used, et cetera. And at a -- at a meeting -- at an advisory meeting, we decided to examine all the archives of the district military prosecutor's office in Zenica, and we decided that if there were any cases that contained interesting information in that respect, we decided that we should re-examine this, re-examine events and the circumstances that prevailed when these cases were dealt with. We decided to re-examine information that wasn't familiar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I also received a case from 1993. There were a few attachments included which had to do with initial information on the events in Dusina at the time of the conflict between ABiH units and HVO units.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The documents that your colleague had from that period, given what you realised when you examined the case, were the documents such that he believed that there was no reason to institute proceedings or had proceedings already been instituted?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the documents consisted of the following: There was information from the security service in Zenica; an examination of 12 or 13 bodies that had been taken to the Zenica hospital morgue; there was the record of the investigating judge - I think that was the judge of the district military court, Vlado Adamovic - there was photo documentation that had been made by the forensics expert; there were the findings, the results of the paraffin glove test; and I think there was an external description of the bodies. That was all the material in the case, and my colleague who worked on the case in 1993 did not believe that this material indicated that a crime had been committed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take any additional steps to reassess the decision of your colleague from 1993?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, because there was information according to which something had happened in Dusina. I contacted the military archives and asked for documents that related to that period, the end of January 1993. I then requested that the organ of the -- of interior affairs find out where some inhabitants from Dusina were located, and I requested that they be interviewed with regard to the circumstances we were interested, with regard to whether civilians had been killed there, women, children, and the elderly, to find out whether prisoners had been killed, whether human shields had been used, to check the information that we were receiving at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I don't want to interrupt the flow of the witness, but because cross-examination will be limited, we hope that he can go over the weekend. If it could be made clear that everything the witness is talking about he did not in 1992 or 1993, he did after the Blaskic trial judgement triggered this new assessment. So it was after 1999. So everybody is clear about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Could you ask the witness when he started re-examining the -- the file. This should be contained in the transcript, because we're not quite sure of the date.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, please tell me when you started to -- when did you exactly start to reassess the case?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: I said that when the trial of General Blaskic started, in the course of his trial. That was perhaps in 1999 or in the year 2000. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And in the course of that year, in accordance with the authorisation that the prosecutor had, you re-examined everything that took place in 1993, and you re-examined the decision taken by your colleague from 1993.

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you receive from the ABiH or the MUP the material that you had requested?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I received from the archives of the ABiH all the material that related to that period, and I received from the MUP a report on an interview with I think three or four Croats. And having examined all the material that I had, I came to the conclusion that a war crime had not been committed in the village of Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did you come to that conclusion having re-examined all the material that your colleague had in 1993, the court records that he had been provided with and all the material, all the information that you subsequently obtained about the event?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I compiled an official report in which I explained all the facts that I had obtained, and I provided a brief analysis of those facts and drew my conclusion. It is true that at one point in time -- well, there was the body of an old man among those bodies. I think he was 77 or 78 years old. So he wasn't a soldier. He wasn't someone fit for military service according to the law. But when I analysed the part of the material, the documents that I had received from the military archives, my conclusion was that this was collateral damage. Unfortunately, it was collateral damage. He was a civilian who happened to be in the area of combat. As far as I can remember in the report that I compiled, my conclusion was that the authorities, the HVO, were far more responsible for his death than anyone else, because if they had expected a conflict to break out and everything points to the fact that a conflict was expected because there was a series of provocations in the wider Dusina area, and therefore it was their duty, it was their responsibility to move the civilians to a safe place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: My last question, Mr. Hadzic, is as follows: The decision you took, was it taken on the basis -- or the decision you took on the basis of the additional information, was it identical to the decision taken by your colleague in 1993? And your colleague also assessed all the material that was accessible to him at the time.

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, my decision was identical to his decision, but I had more voluminous material. I had heard the direct testimony of inhabitants from the village of Dusina, so we came to the same conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before we have our break, does the other Defence team have any questions for this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: No, Your Honours. We don't have any questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. It will be best to have our break now, and we will start with the Prosecution's cross-examination after the break. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. It is now 12.25, and we will resume at about five to one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will now resume, and I give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Hadzic. I just want to clarify a few points with you, and perhaps while I'll ask my first question to you, a few exhibits could be distributed. I won't need all of them but just a few of them. And in fact, the first one I want to talk about would be P332. Everyone in the courtroom is quite familiar with this one because we have discussed it a number of times. It's somewhere in the middle of it. Unfortunately, we didn't have time for tabs. P332. But first let me ask you, Mr. Hadzic, while that's being done, the report --

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'm sorry we couldn't accommodate you further. It's a bundle of different exhibits, and the first one I'm going to talk about is in the middle, the cover sheet to the military district court.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, let me ask you something before. You said you looked at these, the file, the documents, whatever, and you made a report. Can you tell us first, when did you start to look these files? Can you tell us the day or the month or certainly the year after, you know, the Blaskic trial triggered this new review? Tell us, when did you start looking into this whole thing, if you can.

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: I couldn't provide you with an exact date or the exact month. As far as I can remember, it was around 1999 or 2000, but it's important to point out that my final conclusion bore the date when the work was completed on that case. What I know for sure, and that enables me to tell you when the approximate time was, this was when the trial of General Blaskic started.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And who asked you, you specifically, to deal with this issue, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: I've already said. Given the media coverage in general and given what was said in the press about General Blaskic's trial, there was an advisory meeting of the cantonal prosecutor's office, and a decision was reached according to which previous cases that were in the archives should be re-examined. There was no official request. We assessed that these were rumours that had reached the prosecutor's office and it was sufficient to make the prosecutor's office want to focus once more on a case that had already been dealt with and completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, your report, if you recall, when did you file the report and to whom did you file or address your report?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: It wasn't a report of any kind. It was an official record. This was a document compiled by the prosecutor who commented, who provided his final comments on a case. There was no special report, because this is the usual procedure followed in the prosecutor's office. A case is either filed in the archives and it's completed, or judicial investigations are launched, judicial processes instituted, and perhaps a formal indictment is brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to clarify, I'm talking about your work product. Sometime after 1999, six years after the event, this work product, you call it just final comments. You drafted that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And how big was it, how many pages?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: A full two pages, I think. A full two pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And to whom was it addressed?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: It wasn't addressed to anyone. As I have said, the work on the case had been completed. And in order to know the reason for which the work had been completed, it was necessary to have some sort of comment made by the prosecutor who was involved in the case. I was the prosecutor involved in the case. I analysed the material that I had at my disposal. I came to the conclusion that there were no grounds upon which one could institute proceedings. I compiled an official record stating the reasons for which I had drawn that conclusion, and that was the end of my work on the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And where is the report now, or the two-page analysis?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: It's in the archives of the cantonal prosecutor's office in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So we could retrieve it at any time?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: That wouldn't a problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you would assist us in finding that paper?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: If it's necessary for me to assist you, yes, but if I went to the prosecutor's office, I would be going there as a private individual. I no longer work in the prosecutor's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, you talked about that, unlike your colleague in 1993, you had, I believe you said, "direct testimony of inhabitants of the village of Dusina." Now, did you -- I understand from your testimony you did not attach any witness statements to your final analysis; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Witness statements were taken and recorded in the police, and these statements are part of the case. There are certain attachments included in the case. There is the initial police report on the arrival of these bodies in the Zenica hospital morgue towards the end of January or the beginning of February, and there were attachments included with the report. And there was the material that I had collected and my final comment. This was part of the material I had gathered, and there was -- there were the documents from the military forces archives. There were the statements of three or four inhabitants of Croat nationality from Dusina. They had spoken about the events in Dusina at the end of January in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I'll come to those witnesses in a moment. Let me just try to understand something looking at this exhibit which is in front of you, Prosecution Exhibit 332, dated 1 February 1993. Was that this report or the -- the file you had seen when you reassessed the incident in -- sometime after 1999? Do you remember having seen this document? And it's only the cover page. You know, you'll see the annexes, and I take it you have seen the annexes as well, if you have. So my question is: Was that provided to you when you assessed the work of your colleague from 1993?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Since it says the district military court here, I don't believe that this is the document I had. I don't believe that I had this specific document, but I did have a report from the MUP, from the security services in Zenica, which was addressed to the prosecutor's office. But I'm not sure about this document, because the address here is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, then perhaps it's time I asked you the name of the colleague that was concerned with the case in 1993. Who was the person whose work you reviewed six years later?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: In the military prosecutor's office, I think there were seven deputies. I really can't remember who worked on that case in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But that -- his name would be contained in the file which is in your office, or in your former office?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. It had to be, and it would have to be entered in the register where the case was entered, and it also had to be stated on the cover page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you, you said that you reviewed his work product and that you did more than he did. So just going back to what your colleague did, having assessed his job, do you remember whether he went to the crime scene in Dusina at that time to conduct an on-site investigation?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: No. If you look at this material, this is a report about identification of bodies which were brought to the dissecting room of the Zenica hospital after the conflict in the village of Dusina, after the clearing of the terrain after the combat operations. My colleague did not go to Dusina. I myself didn't go either for one simple reason: As a prosecutor, I was just asking for facts to be re-checked to determine in a different way whether a crime had been committed in Dusina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you're confident to say that also your colleague in 1993, or anybody else connected to him which would have been reflected in his work product, did not go to Dusina?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: In the material that I had, there was no information about that. And to respond to the second part of your previous question, I did go into a slightly broader investigation than my colleague did in 1993. That's a fact, because the reports or the information that we were receiving, information that there were casualties for no reason in the village of Dusina, for us this was sufficient reason to re-examine that case and to re-check whether this information, these reports that we were receiving were correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thanks for your answer, and I want to come to your role in a moment, but let me go back to your colleague of 1993. You said you didn't see any record of a visit to the possible crime scene, and you also told us at the end of your testimony this morning and after the break as well that you interviewed some people from Dusina. Now, your colleague in 1993, he did not interview people, inhabitants from Dusina; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Let us first clarify one thing. I did not directly speak with the inhabitants of Dusina. I instructed the police to find several survivors from Dusina who were accessible and to interview them. And based on the statements that they give to the police, I as prosecutor would evaluate whether there were grounds to continue with the proceedings. I don't know if my colleague did the same thing in 1993. I know what I found in the case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in the case file, you did not see any record of any interviewing of witnesses by your colleague or by the MUP or by the military; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: No. There were no subjective pieces of evidence in the case file. There were no witness statements or not -- no information about possible witnesses either.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And in your knowledge as a prosecutor, expert in this field, if he had interviewed any witnesses or anybody else at that time, would that have been reflected in the file, in the record, the dossier?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Everything that is done has to be in the case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you about an intriguing comment you made this morning at the end and the information you had about what happened in Dusina. Now, in your recollection, and you were quite specific about provocation and other military activities, in your recollection, were HVO soldiers taken captive on that day, on the 26th of February, 1993, by the ABiH army? January. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Which HVO soldiers are you thinking of? This question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, I'm merely asking you, because you displayed some knowledge about the military activities, whether the ABiH army who was present in Dusina has captured HVO soldiers. In reviewing these documents - and you said you had access to the military archives - did you see any HVO soldiers, perhaps also civilians, Croat civilians, I don't know, being captured in or around Dusina on that day in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know about civilians. As far as captured HVO members, yes, there were such cases. I mentioned that part of the material which I compiled later was also a videotape in which when we played it you could see the medical or the ambulances are bringing over together wounded HVO soldiers and wounded ABiH army soldiers. What specifically interested me here was the cause of death of these persons who had been brought to the dissecting department of the Zenica hospital. That was the part that I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, let me come to other possible avenues which one could have looked at when determining whether a crime was occurring. I believe you said you interviewed -- or on your behalf witnesses were interviewed. Now, you also told us that in Blaskic, or you followed perhaps the Blaskic judgement. In deciding whom to interview or whom to ask to be interviewed, did you look at the Blaskic record who testified in the Blaskic case and who could have any information perhaps on what happened to these HVO soldiers who were arrested? Did you check Blaskic witnesses?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, work on this case didn't begin after the judgement was passed in the Blaskic case but after the beginning of the trial. Second, you must understand that we didn't have access, the security services centre in Zenica did not have access to all witnesses, all the inhabitants of Dusina, but there were several inhabitants who had come to Zenica or its environs, and I asked that as many as possible of these inhabitants from Dusina be found so that we could interview them. They were found and interviewed, and based on the information that they gave, I concluded what I concluded. So as far as the Blaskic case file, at that point in time it wasn't of any particular interest to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Now, did you interview survivors of these events if they were, according to your information, in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. I asked that the inhabitants of Dusina village who happened to be in the village who were the eyewitnesses to these events be interviewed. That was my instruction to the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Did you interview Ivica Kegelj, for instance? Was born 1957, could have told you everything about what happened to these HVO soldiers. Do you remember having given an assignment to interview him?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: I don't think that you understood me at all. After the conflict, the Croats from the village of Dusina dispersed. A large number of them went to neighbouring Busovaca and generally to the areas which were held by the HVO, so they were not accessible for us. I don't know where Ivica Kegelj went. Since I knew this fact that all Dusina inhabitants are not accessible to us, I asked that information be collected from those individuals whom we did have access to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you knew about the name of Ivica Kegelj and that he was a survivor when you assessed your information?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. I mentioned the name of Ivica Kegelj after your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So you have never heard of him?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: I do not remember him, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Not to this day? How about --

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: I'm trying, but I really cannot remember, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: How about Zvonko Rajic [sic]? She was the wife of Mr. Rajic who was present when her husband was killed in Dusina that day. Have you tried to locate her? In fact, have you heard of the name of the wife of Zvonko Rajic when you reviewed the work of your colleague?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: No. Her name was not in the case file.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And you also didn't hear that in the Blaskic trial, in open testimony, she testified that her husband was taken away by an ABiH battalion commander and then killed? You have not reviewed that transcript?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: As far as you can believe newspaper articles now, I personally officially did not have any such information, but this was all checked. And if her testimony had pointed to the possibility that a criminal act had been committed, I'm sure that the prosecutor would have continued the proceedings along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Who were the ABiH army units present on the 26th of January, 1993, in Dusina?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: You're asking for too many details. All this information I did have through the documents from the archives, but I cannot recall all of the units of the B and H army which were in the broader area of the village of Dusina and in Dusina itself. In any case, according to the material that I had, you could easily reconstruct which units were there, but I myself don't remember which ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Have you interviewed any of the commanders who might have given you information about what happened to these HVO soldiers who were captured? Have you interviewed any commander?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Generally what I know about captured HVO members, not only from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that particular conflict but from other conflicts, too, most of them were exchanged. In this specific case, what I was interested in was the following: During the conflict in the village of Dusina, were there any civilian casualties unjustified of -- by war? Were there any thefts or looting or anything that would violate international law? Were any prisoners killed? Were human shields used? These were the things that I was looking at and the information that we were receiving. The cause was to examine the cause of death of these people who had been brought to the dissecting room of the Zenica hospital. Therefore, I didn't need to speak with members of the army, of the B and H army, because I had the correspondence amongst the units and the commands from the archive. At that point, I was interested whether the attack was planned, whether assault operations were planned, what was the objective, and what needed to be done. I did not find an order which would indicate that an attack was supposed to be carried out. But chronologically, when you sorted the documents of the B and H army that I had, you could see that this was a pretty sensitive area and that this was part of some kind of general rule, a result of a series of tensions and different incidents, open conflict between the HVO and the B and H army. From the point of view of possible criminal responsibility, it was necessary to see whether the attack was planned, and if it was planned, was it carried out, and then during this assault operations, was there any unjustified -- were there any unjustified casualties among the civilians. So this was the topic of my interest in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just sum up. In the situation where obviously something has happened, and you referred to the report of the physical description of the bodies, and we have no time to go into that; where you say you have heard or read in documents that HVO soldiers were captured; third, that an old man was collateral damage because he was unfortunate enough to be in the area, you did not feel it necessary to talk to the commander on the field to give you some information about what happened to these captured HVO soldiers? You thought that wasn't necessary, six years after the event.

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Six years after the event, I have to go back again to what I said before. As far as the army was concerned, I had official documents, and the subjective explanation of a commander, some commanders, or all commanders at that point was not relevant to me because I was interested in the consequences. This was a military conflict in which two armed formations clashed. Please allow me to finish. This was a military conflict in which two armed formations clashed, in which, unfortunately, soldiers do have the right to kill each other and wound each other, unfortunately, but the death of this gentleman who was about 70-odd years old and whose body was brought to the dissecting room of the Zenica hospital, to me personally, when I was analysing the case file, was interesting because he was not a military conscript and because in his case, when the paraffin glove test was conducted on him, there were no traces of gun powder found on his hands. In all the other cases, these traces were found. To me this was proof that they took part in the military conflict and that they carried weapons and that they fired them. And earlier I said that unfortunately soldiers from opposing sides have the right to kill and wound each other. On the other hand, the cause of death of this elderly gentleman, my assessment in that case was that unfortunately he happened to be in a combat zone. The civilian authorities were the ones who were supposed to take care of the security of civilians. And if combat operations are imminent, then the military organs in that area are responsible. So in this case, the elderly gentleman died in the area of responsibility of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Anyway, let me ask you, if you recall, who told you about the circumstances under which this old man died? Can you give us a name?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: No one spoke about the circumstances to me in which this elderly gentleman - I think his surname was Kegelj died. No one told me anything about the circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: That's your job to find out.

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, look, when I asked the police to determine the cause of death for these individuals and to establish the other facts that I was interested in - I won't repeat everything - the murder of civilians, children, women and -- et cetera, when I requested such information, I asked them to determine the cause of death of this elderly gentleman, Mr. Kegelj. But you must understand the circumstances, the conditions under which we were living at the time. It was still very difficult to reach the territory under HVO control, which used to be Herceg-Bosna. It was difficult to talk to people there, locate them, bring them to testify, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just clear this one point up. Dusina wasn't at that time under HVO control, and we have even people from Zenica, from the municipal protection, who went there the day after. Have you heard about that? That they went to Dusina late January 1993 to collect the bodies.

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, that's the duty of the civilian protection, to clear up the terrain. And if anyone went there, they went there in an official capacity, that's for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me ask you: How many times did you have collateral damage, in your words, in those days, those months you were concerned with? Was that something normal or was that something unusual?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Any civilian casualty is an unusual casualty, and I wouldn't comment on the context of your question, but there was a lot of collateral damage in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And as far as the cases that I worked on myself, I never came across something that would lead me to such a conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So that would be something unusual. Wouldn't you then try to do whatever you can to resolve this issue? Question number one; and second question: Who is the first person you want to ask about any military action who would have led to collateral damage? Who is the person you want to know about? Question number two.

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Your first question is -- could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: The first question is: Wasn't that something unusual, then, if it's the first time you heard about that? So I take --

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Let me answer the first question immediately. When I examined the file, when I examined the attachments to the file, I noticed that among those who had been killed - these were young people - I noticed that there was an elderly gentleman among them, and I tried to determine the causes of his death. I tried to look into the matter. I did everything that I could do in accordance with the law, and I did everything that I was supposed to do within my service. But everything I did pointed to the fact that this elderly gentleman, Mr. Kegelj, had died in the course of an intense conflict. I've already commented on my official record. I have said that the others had gunpowder traces on their hands. That means that they were involved in the fight, as I have already said. Unfortunately, soldiers have the right to kill each other, and unfortunately those are the consequences of each and every war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Exactly. And the responsibility for causing collateral damage, that's the military. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. I do agree with you. And in my comment with regard to the death of Mr. Kegelj, I said that I held the HVO authorities accountable for his death. Since they had been expecting a conflict to break out, they did not try to move civilians out of the area in which fighting was going to take place. That was my conclusion. And when fire is opened indiscriminately, it's impossible to control the directions that bullets will be fired in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the basis for all these conclusions, quite elaborate, are the documents. You did not talk to the military commander. For instance, Mr. Serif Paskovic, who was the 2nd Battalion commander, has documents which you may have seen revealed. You did not talk to Mr. Serif Paskovic; is that correct? I believe you said it before. You had not contacts with the military command, just to confirm it.

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: That's correct, but you're forgetting the role of a prosecutor. Up until the law on criminal proceedings, which is now in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the Prosecutor did not conduct an investigation. He didn't have the right to interview anyone. The Prosecutor would receive information via organs whose responsibility it was to provide him with information. As for an official investigation, all the subject, if evidence was presented, collated by the investigating judge. I as the prosecutor didn't have the authority to summon anyone to an interview. As far as assessing whether it would be necessary to speak to some of the unit commanders, if I had believed that there were elements indicating a crime had committed, then I'm sure such a person would have been interviewed, either as a suspect or as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: You said this morning, and I quote you, "A prosecutor's duty is, quote, He's obliged to check the grounds for the information in relation to authenticity and reliability of facts so he can assess whether there are sufficient grounds." Of course you have a duty, a duty and the authority to ask, request more information if the investigating judge doesn't do his job. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: No, you're not on the right path. The investigating judge only starts working after the prosecutor has determined that there are elements indicating that crime has been committed. He formulates a request for an investigation, which is then forwarded to the investigating judge. The investigating judge then has to interview the suspect, and then he has to take a decision on implementing an investigation, carry out the investigative measures that the prosecutor has requested and he believes that should be carried out, and then he forwards this to the prosecutor. What was done was done in the pre-trial phase. It means that the information that we received was checked in order to determine whether there were grounds for suspicion and whether there were grounds for making a request to carry out an investigation. The investigating judge was at the site. He was in the Zenica hospital, and he identified these bodies. That's the only thing that he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just quote what you just told us. You said that, "The investigative judge, in implementing an investigation, he has to carry out the investigative measures that the prosecutor has requested." So if you receive a file from the investigative authorities about the collateral damage case and you don't see any attempt to talk to the military commander on the ground, especially since he has been mentioned now in the Blaskic trial as being the killer, perpetrator, by an eyewitness, surely you would refuse to even give an assessment before the investigative judge does his job. Am I not correct?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: You haven't understood me. According to the procedure, according to the criminal procedure -- well, this procedure is quite different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since I examined the witness for 32 minutes and the -- my colleague has been examining the witness for 43 minutes, I would like to know whether my learned friend will be asking for more time so that we can know whether this witness will be completing his testimony today or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Because in theory, we should adjourn in four minutes' time. How much more time do you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I believe I'm about to finish. Perhaps five minutes, with your leave, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I continue? The investigative judge only gets involved in the criminal procedure after the prosecutor has made a request for an investigation, and this is the third time that I will repeat this. This is the third time I will try to clarify this. Although this raises a number of legal issues, the prosecutor makes a request for an investigation when he believes that the material he has at his disposal provides grounds upon which one can draw the conclusion that a certain individual committed a crime. When investigating this case, my task was to determine whether a war crime had been committed in Dusina and to determine who the perpetrator was. The conclusion I reached was that a war crime had not been committed in Dusina and this is why an official investigation was never launched. So please don't try to involve the investigating judge in this matter. In this case, the investigating judge didn't play any role whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Let me just finish on this point and overall. If this was indeed a war crime, who would be the possible suspect? Although you said it was the HVO, but let's assume for a moment that these HVO prisoners were kept, captured by the ABiH soldiers, as military documents which I'm sure you have looked at indicate, and these people were killed, executed, not collateral damage but executed, who would be the primary suspect of this case?
