utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If these individuals --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The question is leading. The question is not leading, but my colleague is not correctly referring to the army documents. None of the army documents states that these individuals who were killed had been captured. In the army documents, what is stated is quite different, and you are aware of the fact because all three documents have been admitted into evidence. So it's not possible to suggest things to the witness if they have no grounds in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Mr. President, first of all, I did not say that it happened like that. I said let's assume that it happened, number one. And second, we have evidence that the HVO soldiers were captured on that day. I think it's five to six. There are at least three documents that suggest that, contemporaneous documents. So I'm asking him because he claimed that these HVO soldiers were, you know -- or the HVO was responsible for these elderly men. I'm asking him just in his capacity who the usual suspect would be in a case like that.

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Well, if we're discussing this as a hypothesis, if we assume that these seven individuals were captured alive and after they had been disarmed they were killed, then first the immediate or direct perpetrator would be responsible and then his superior. So that's an assumption. But based on the documents that I had, these individuals died in combat. They were killed in combat. When examining these bodies, there are no traces of violence, either while they were alive or either after they had been killed. The cause of death was an entry and exit wound in the case of all of them, apart from one individual who had been wounded in the head, and that was probably the result of the explosion of a shell, a hand grenade, or something like that. So according to the documents that I had, these individuals were killed in combat. When they were killed, they were armed. They had been opening fire at army members, and there were no civilians, no women or children who -- who were killed subsequently. That's what I managed to establish on the basis of the material that I had. Those are the conclusions that I reached.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: And the witnesses you talked to to come to this conclusion would be mentioned in your two-page assessment?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: The witness statements that the police had recorded are contained in the file, and I interpreted these statements in my report, but these original statements are in the file, because I didn't reach this decision off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Just to conclude, because you mentioned this report about the physical description of these bodies and the belief, you said, that they had an exit wound -- an entry wound and an exit wound. How many entry wounds and exit wounds do you remember that these bodies had, if you recall?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: First of all, I didn't say that. I didn't mention entry and exit wounds. I talked about gunshot wounds. My conclusion is based on what I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. found based on the findings of the doctors. The forensic processing of the bodies or -- indicated that there were no gunpowder rings at the entry wounds - now I am mentioning them - which would indicate that they had been shot at from close range.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Yes, I wasn't asking about that, although we can come to that in a second. I was asking about for these bodies, because you talked about these entry wounds - at least that's what the transcript says - do you recall, because you were interested about the cause of death, you said, do you recall how many bullets penetrated or at least reached these bodies? Just whatever you recall. Was it just one or was it more?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: I described in detail what I recall. I recall this grave injury to the head. I know that according to the medical findings I established that the cause of death was a small calibre firearm. I don't know how many wounds there were on each individual body. I cannot remember that. But the photographs taken of these persons exist, and they were photographed according to all forensic rules and regulations, proper records and exhibits were made. But I really cannot recall how many wounds each individual body had sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: But it's possible that there were bodies among these bodies which had multiple, I mean five and more, exit and entry wounds on both sides of the body, meaning on the same side both exit and entry wound. Do you remember that, having seen that?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: For that part, I can only say that I looked at the medical findings which were part of the case file. The doctor who examined the bodies established the number of wounds, the location of the wounds, and ultimately this is really not my job. This is not a legal but a medical question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: So just to be sure, you don't remember a body which has been riddled by bullets? You don't remember that?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: No, I really cannot remember. I told you just a few of the most striking details that stuck with me. I have been a prosecutor for over 20 years, and I've had more than 4.000 cases during that time, so -- many more serious crimes that I had looked at, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Well, I would be looking forward to seeing these more serious cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Hadzic, in order to clarify the situation, the colleague asked you several times whether you were aware that there were captured HVO soldiers, and you replied that from the army documents you saw that there were some captured HVO soldiers. Please, the documents that you found in the case file and the documents that you compiled indicated and in what manner did it indicate that these dead persons were amongst the captured persons? Did you find any information or data which would indicate that the persons who were killed were captured?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: You mean that they had been captured first and then -- no, no. There was no such data. Everything that I had in the case file indicated that they were killed during the combat operations.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that you had a record by the investigative judge, Vlado Adamovic, in the case file. Could you please tell me, when in the earlier procedure, when does the investigative judge go out into the field and who handles or who is in charge of this on-site investigation, and who instructs all the relevant organs which actions are supposed to be carry out in case of the procedure?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: When we're conducting an on-site inquiry or any other procedure which is in the presence of the investigative judge, then he's the one who is in charge of the whole operations, and his instructions are binding on all the parties who take part in that particular inquiry.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If the prosecutor is also present or the civilian police or the military police in that same inquiry, are they in a position to conduct independent activities or must they behave in accordance with instructions of the investigative judge?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: They must behave in accordance with the investigative judge, and they can also propose just that some activities are carried out, but it's up to the investigative judge to accept that or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: How many times have you tried to clarify to my learned friend the role of the investigative judge and the prosecutor in criminal proceedings? This part which you reviewed, as well as that part which was conducted by your colleague in 1993 when he received the material, was this a formal procedure, an investigative procedure, or was this a pre-trial procedure which was not in the formal investigation stage at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: I was very precise in one of the last questions that the Prosecutor put to me. What I did and what my colleague did from 1993 was at the so-called pre-trial stage, which is not formalised in a court investigation.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At that stage, during the pre-trial proceedings when the prosecutor has all the material and is assessing and evaluating it, who is the dominus litis? Who manages the procedure, and who instructs the other organs to carry out other steps?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: This would be the prosecutor. He's the one who's in charge of the proceedings, and all the -- all the instructions that he issues to all the other organs in the investigation are binding.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your colleague in 1993, when he had this material in his position -- possession, if he had any doubts about the cause of death, would he be the only authorised organ to request additional steps from other bodies; state bodies, police bodies, or any other ones?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Only him and no one else, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you assess, and at this point in time you did not assess that you had enough -- sufficient grounds for formal proceedings, but when you assess that there are sufficient grounds to embark on a formal procedure and then this is handed over to the investigative judge, then who handles the proceedings? Who calls witnesses? Who issues instructions about further steps? Who is the person then who can ask other subjects to contribute to a clarification of that matter?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Up until the -- from the point in time that an investigation is initiated, the investigative judge is the one who is in charge. He's the one who handles the case. The investigative judge calls witnesses, questions them, questions the accused, orders inquiries, on-site investigations. He issues other instructions. So he undertakes all the investigative activities or instructs that they be carried out, up until the point in time that the investigation is completed

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I would just like you to wait until my question is completely interpreted before you begin answering. My colleague asked you several questions about the wounds and injuries and I would like to ask you the following: When you looked at the photographs and read the description of the wounds given by the doctor, who is the only qualified person to do that, those injuries and their description, were they any different or more unusual than other injuries sustained in wartime that you had been able to see for yourself or that you encountered in other cases?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: There was nothing unusual about them. I would just like -- just one second, I'm waiting for the interpretation to finish. There was nothing unusual about those wounds, including their location. See, the bodies were photographed naked. All the clothing was removed and then the bodies were placed on the autopsy tables and photographed. So the photographs were made according to the proper procedure, from several angles, several positions. The doctor conducted an external investigation, established the death and the causes of death; and for me that was enough to believe that the wounds were gunshot wounds except for this one very serious head wound. But even that, even though it was extremely grave, was something that was usual in times of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In several questions it was suggested that you could have done more based on the information you had and the testimony from the Blaskic case. The canton prosecutor's office in Zenica at the time when you were reviewing this case, did it have access to the transcript from that case? Was it possible to have something like that in Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time or were you acting at the time based on information which was sporadically published in the newspapers?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: We decided to look at the archives of the earlier district military prosecutor's office based on TV reports and newspaper articles. We didn't have a transcript from the trial. We didn't have the indictments. We didn't have any of the exhibits used in the Blaskic case. At the time, we were not in a position to have something like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And finally, my learned friend asked you whether you listened to the testimony of Zvonko Rajic's wife who claimed that Serif Paskovic killed her husband. I -- of course you responded to that question. What I'm asking you now is the following: As a citizen of Zenica, are you following the proceedings against Hakanovic, and do you know that Zvonko Rajic's wife gave a completely different statement before that court than the one she gave in the Blaskic case?

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that from information published in the press about the Hakanovic trial.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution is on its feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. WAESPI
utterances.text: I think that was improper. I don't think re-examination is time to ask leading questions, and she was testifying and saying, you know, Were you aware... She could have asked, you know, have you heard that she gave somewhere else testimony and then he could have answered. I don't think that's proper.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours, we have no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As far as I'm concerned, I would like to put some questions to you, but since we don't have much time, I'll just put one minor question to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One member of the Zenica police force established a report on the state of the bodies. We could show you this report. It was signed by Redzo Hadzic. Is this a relative of yours or is this just a homonym? We could show you the document. The document is number 333.

utterances.speaker: RAGIB HADZIC
utterances.text: It's not necessary. I know the document in question. Mr. Redzo Hadzic, unfortunately he has died in the meantime, was not a relative of mine, but I can say that he was an exceptionally good forensics expert in the Zenica security service, but we happened to have the same family name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. There are no other questions. Thank you for having come to The Hague to testify. We have worked for a little longer than usual, but it was necessary to put all the questions to you. I wish you a good trip home, and I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very briefly could the Defence inform us of the schedule for next week.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go into private session? I forgot to mention this earlier on.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session. Today's hearing is over. It is now 14.05. I apologise to the interpreters that we worked longer than the time we were allotted, but there was no other way. I am recalling everybody back on Monday for the continuation of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. our hearing at 14.15 hours.
